title: Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment?
description:
Nov 10, 2026 11:25am PT	
	

	
	Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment?
body:
Nov 10, 2026 11:25am PT	
	

	
	Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment?
	



			
			
	
						

									©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection
	
					


							
		
	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change in response to buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.
	



	

					DISCLOSURE DAY, foreground, first four from left: Colman Domingo, Tommy Martinez, Emily Blunt, Josh O’Connor; far right: Priyanka Kedia, 2026. © Universal Pictures / courtesy Everett Collection
									©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection
	




	Best Original Score Predictions Commentary (Updated: Nov. 10, 2026): Multiple Oscar winners, potential breakout composers and overdue artisans are overflowing this year’s original score category.

	“The Odyssey” composer Ludwig Göransson is coming in with a perfect score (pun intended), having already collected three statuettes for “Black Panther” (2018), “Oppenheimer” (2023) and “Sinners” (2025). Will they give the 42-year-old Swedish-born musician another one?After winning his second Oscar for “Dune” (2021) — a long-overdue triumph following “The Lion King” (1994) — Hans Zimmer is entering this season with high expectations. After being ineligible for “Dune: Part Two,” the German composer is said to have developed new, original cues for Denis Villeneuve’s highly anticipated conclusion, due out in December.

	It would be foolish to count out 94-year-old legendary composer John Williams, who is collaborating once again with Steven Spielberg on the sci-fi drama “Disclosure Day.” With 54 Oscar nominations — the second-most of any person in history behind Walt Disney—Williams is also the oldest Academy Award nominee in any category, a record he has broken three times himself. The last was at age 91, when he picked up his nomination for “Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny” (2023). Another one could easily be on the way.

	All eyes are on English musician Daniel Pemberton this year, whose long history of stunning, iconic work has largely gone overlooked and unrewarded. Despite groundbreaking music in films such as “Steve Jobs” (2015), “Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse” (2018) and “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse” (2023), his sole Oscar nomination came as a songwriter for “Hear My Voice” from “The Trial of the Chicago 7” (2020). This year, he’s contributing to six different films: “The Bad Guys 2,” “The Drama,” “Ink,” “Masters of the Universe,” “Musk” and “Project Hail Mary.”

	He already received an honor this season, taking home the Distinguished Composer Award at the Middleburg Film Festival, where he also performed live with a full orchestra, bringing the Salamander Resort to its feet. It got me thinking: Could this finally be the year Pemberton wins an Oscar?
	

	Furthermore, “Project Hail Mary,” which is shaping up to be a major nominee across the board, is running into what looks to be an epic duel between two other technical juggernauts: “Dune: Part Three” and “The Odyssey.” The original score category has historically served as a consolation prize for Best Picture contenders. Just look at “Atonement” (Dario Marianelli, 2007), “Babel” (Gustavo Santaolalla, 2006), “Finding Neverland” (Jan A.P. Kaczmarek, 2004) and “The Full Monty” (Anne Dudley, 1997). If the film manages to make the cut across the board, this would be a fantastic way to reward it.

	But again, it’s early. It’s only November, and there’s still a long way to go. Any of the potential breakouts and newcomers, including Raül Refree (“La Bola Negra”), Damon Albarn (“Artificial”), Ari Balouzian (“You Can See Everything”) and Devonté Hynes (“The Invite”), could make their cases. Other well-established veterans like Randy Newman (“Toy Story 5”), Michael Giacchino (“Ray Gunn”) and Alberto Iglesias (“Bitter Christmas”) could also pop up.

	And with a relatively small number of female composers in the conversation, we should keep an eye on Rebekka Karijord (“Tenzing”), Natalie Holt (“Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom”), Hildur Guðnadóttir (“28 Years Later: The Bone Temple”), Isobel Waller-Bridge (“The Unknown”) and Tara Nome Doyle (“Rose”) to make a play.

	The list of predictions in all categories can be found here.

	The Governors Awards, which will hand out honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, will take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscars shortlist in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlist announcement to follow Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, 2026, nominations voting will run Jan. 11-15, 2027. The official Oscar nominations will be announced on Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars will take place on Sunday, March 14, 2027 and will be hosted by Conan O’Brien. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.
	



	

					TENZING, from left: Genden Phuntsok as Tenzing Norgay, Tom Hiddleston as Edmund Hillary, Willem Dafoe as Colonel John Hunt, Benjamin Hoetjes, 2026. ph: Kirsty Griffin / © Apple TV+ / Courtesy Everett Collection
									©Apple TV/Courtesy Everett Collection

title: Shaq to Star in Hide-and-Seek Competition Series ‘Can You Hide… Shaq?’ at ABC (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Many have played hide-and-seek. But few have played hide-and-Shaq.

	A new competition series at ABC asks the question, “Can You Hide… Shaq?” Hoste
body:
Many have played hide-and-seek. But few have played hide-and-Shaq.

	A new competition series at ABC asks the question, “Can You Hide… Shaq?” Hosted by comedian Nicole Byer, the show will follow eight contestants as they attempt to hide the gargantuan NBA legend in plain sight in Dallas. They’ll have to disguise, distract and deceive for a shot at grand prize money.

	The series will premiere with two episodes on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 9 p.m. on ABC and the ESPN app. Episodes will stream on Hulu the next day.
	

	“I’m 7-foot-1. I’m not exactly easy to miss,” said Shaquille O’Neal in a statement. “I love meeting people wherever I go, but for years I’ve always wondered, could somebody actually make me disappear? Well, we finally decided to put it to the test. We turned it into a real competition, and I can’t wait for you to see the creative, ridiculous ways they tried to hide me in plain sight. The stakes are high, and so is the prize. But you know me, we’re gonna have some fun along the way.”

	Per the series logline, “In the fast, funny and unpredictable challenges, contestants first split into two teams, each with a set mission and time clock. The team that completes its mission with the fewest spottings earns immunity for one team member in the next round, who then becomes team captain. The teams must work together toward one greater mission: earning prize money to add to the ‘Shaq-pot’ that will ultimately be claimed by one winner.”

	“Can You Hide… Shaq?” is produced by Fulwell Entertainment and Jersey Legends Productions, in partnership with ESPN. O’Neal, Ben Winston, Colin Smeeton, Mike Parris, Jeremy Castro, Emma Conway, Charlie Van Vleet, Shyam Balse, Adam Cooper and Byer serve as executive producers.

schema.headline: Shaq to Star in Hide-and-Seek Competition Series ‘Can You Hide… Shaq?’ at ABC (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘The Peanut Butter Falcon’ Breakout Zack Gottsagen and Anna Enger Ritch to Star in ‘A Reason to Stay’ From Director Rippin Sindher (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “The Peanut Butter Falcon” breakout Zack Gottsagen and “S.W.A.T.” star Anna Enger Ritch will star as brother and sister in “A Reason to Stay,” a ne
body:
“The Peanut Butter Falcon” breakout Zack Gottsagen and “S.W.A.T.” star Anna Enger Ritch will star as brother and sister in “A Reason to Stay,” a new romantic comedy from Rippin Sindher. The film recently wrapped principal photography in Ohio. 

	The project reunites Gottsagen with TVACOM Films’ Davied Thiews after their collaboration on “The Peanut Butter Falcon.” Kelli A. White of With-An-i Productions also serves as producer alongside Promised The Moon Productions. Additional producers include Amy Russ, Melanie Forchetti, William Thies and Katie Cassidy. Ridley Scott, Archie Panjabi, Sonein Noack and Emik David serve as executive producers.
	

	Per an official logline, “A Reason to Stay,” which Sindher co-wrote with Melanie Forchetti, follows “Zach (Gottsagen), a young man with Down syndrome who helps run his family’s struggling animal shelter alongside his sister Sophie (Ritch), who returns home following their mother’s death. As Sophie confronts the life she left behind, an unexpected reunion with a former love forces her to decide whether to return to the future she planned or embrace a second chance at home.” Spencer Neville also stars.

	After breaking out with her 2025 short, “Flight 182,” Sindher makes her feature directorial debut with “A Reason to Stay.” In April, she was named as one of seven fellows for the Sundance Institute’s Cultural Impact Residency.

	“This is a universal film about families we build and the power of people coming together for something bigger than themselves,” said producer White. “Zack has an extraordinary ability to bring honesty and emotional truth to the screen, and Rippin is exactly the kind of filmmaker who can honor that while making a film that feels cinematic, funny and deeply human.”
	

	Gottsagen made his big-screen debut starring alongside Shia LaBeouf and Dakota Johnson in “The Peanut Butter Falcon.” His most recent film credit was the 2025 Netflix thriller “Night Always Comes” with Vanessa Kirby. Ritch is probably best known for her roles as Zoe Powell on CBS’ “S.W.A.T.” and Joey on Netflix’s “The Haunting of Hill House.” Her last big-screen role was in Prime Video’s 2023 drama film “On a Wing and a Prayer,” which starred Dennis Quaid and Heather Graham. 

	Gottsagen is repped by Advanced Management. Ritch is repped by the Joseph Le Talent Agency. Neville is repped by Innovative Artists.

schema.headline: ‘The Peanut Butter Falcon’ Breakout Zack Gottsagen and Anna Enger Ritch to Star in ‘A Reason to Stay’ From Director Rippin Sindher (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Legendary Entertainment Hires Apollo Partner Aaron Sobel (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Legendary Entertainment, the company behind “Dune” and “Godzilla,” has hired Apollo partner Aaron Sobel. 

	He will serve as a member of Legendary’
body:
Legendary Entertainment, the company behind “Dune” and “Godzilla,” has hired Apollo partner Aaron Sobel. 

	He will serve as a member of Legendary’s senior management team, helping lead and execute the strategy including corporate development, M&A, capital strategy and formation, and overseeing new business initiatives. He will report directly to Josh Grode, CEO of Legendary.

	Sobel’s newly created role is intended to expand Legendary’s ability to pursue opportunities across media and entertainment. His hiring comes as Legendary has reportedly been pursuing an acquisition of Lionsgate.
	

	“I have worked closely with Aaron for the past four years and seen firsthand his exceptional strategic judgment, understanding of our business and genuine belief in Legendary,” said Grode. “As we build on a period of meaningful creative and commercial success, bringing Aaron into our leadership team will help us execute the next stage of our long-term growth strategy. His experience and business acumen will be invaluable as we expand into new areas.”

	Sobel joins Legendary after 15 years at Apollo, where he served as a partner in the firm’s private equity business and worked in investments across media, entertainment and telecommunications. Before joining Apollo in 2011, he worked in the Investment Banking Division at Goldman Sachs. Sobel has been named to Private Equity International’s “Future 40: Dealmakers” list and Variety’s annual Variety500 list of the most influential leaders in the global media industry. 

	“Having worked closely with Josh, Mary Parent and the Legendary team through Apollo funds’ investment in the company, I have seen the strength of the business and the quality of its leadership,” said Sobel. “The team has developed an ambitious long-term growth strategy, and I could not be more excited to join Legendary and work alongside them to bring that vision to life. This is an opportunity to contribute more directly to a company I know well and deeply believe in.”
	

	Legendary’s upcoming slate includes “Dune: Part Three,” “Godzilla x Kong: Supernova” and a sequel to “A Minecraft Movie.” The company is also working on “Gundam,” a live-action adaptation of the iconic Japanese franchise, starring Sydney Sweeney and Noah Centineo.

schema.headline: Legendary Entertainment Hires Apollo Partner Aaron Sobel (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Alexander Skarsgård, Hunter Schafer, Maya Hawke, Harry Melling to Star in ‘The Confessions,’ With Ari Aster Producing (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Alexander Skarsgård (“Wicker”), Hunter Schafer (“Blade Runner 2099”), Maya Hawke (“Stranger Things”) and Harry Melling (“Pillion”) are set to star
body:
Alexander Skarsgård (“Wicker”), Hunter Schafer (“Blade Runner 2099”), Maya Hawke (“Stranger Things”) and Harry Melling (“Pillion”) are set to star in “The Confessions,” the latest feature from Canadian filmmaking trio Guy Maddin, Galen Johnson and Evan Johnson, with Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg producing.

	The project, which marks the trio’s follow-up to their Cannes-premiering political satire “Rumours,” is being launched at the AFM by CAA Media Finance and WME Independent, which are co-representing North American rights, and French sales company Charades, which is handling international sales.
	

	Described as a cautionary psycho-dramedy, “The Confessions” follows a group of condemned nuns bearing witness to the accursed, globe-spanning love triangle of a missing sea captain and his poet wife.

	The film reunites Maddin and the Johnson brothers with Square Peg, which boarded the project in early development after collaborating with the filmmakers on “Rumours,” which premiered out of competition at Cannes in 2024. Daniel Bekerman’s Scythia Films has also joined the project.

	“The Confessions” is produced by Square Peg in the U.S., Scythia Films and Galen Johnson, Evan Johnson and Fritzi Adelman’s Thin Stuff in Canada, with the support of Telefilm Canada.

	Square Peg’s credits include “Bugonia,” “Midsommar” and “The Drama,” while Scythia Films is behind “The Witch,” “The Apprentice” and “Falling.” Thin Stuff’s credits include “Rumours,” “A.Rimbaud” and “Strong Son.”
	

	“I have long been a devoted fan of the great Canadian wizard, Guy Maddin, and his equally brilliant partners, Evan and Galen Johnson,” said Aster. “They stand humongously tall among my favorite filmmakers in the world, and The Confessions is as singular and beguiling as anything they’ve ever written.”

	Known for their surrealist, genre-bending storytelling, Maddin and the Johnson brothers made their first feature together with “Rumours,” an absurdist political comedy starring Cate Blanchett, Alicia Vikander and Charles Dance that follows world leaders who become lost in the woods during a G7 summit.

	“Behold, I will do a new thing! Now it shall spring forth!” So sayeth the Bible. (Isaiah 43:19) But our film, part religio-maritime rough-music psychomachy, part hallucinated saltwater shaming parade, has Alex, Hunter, Harry, and Maya on its side, in its belly, so we are already several steps ahead of the Bible. Behold!,” said the filmmaker in an eccentric statement. 

	Elevation Pictures will distribute “The Confessions” in Canada.

schema.headline: Alexander Skarsgård, Hunter Schafer, Maya Hawke, Harry Melling to Star in ‘The Confessions,’ With Ari Aster Producing (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Harry Potter’ Star Paapa Essiedu Says ‘I Don’t Want to Talk About’ J.K. Rowling ‘At All’ but ‘Trans People Have the Right to Be Treated With Respect and Dignity’
description: HBO‘s “Harry Potter” showrunner Francesca Gardiner is condemning the “abuse” being directed at Paapa Essiedu, the “I May Destroy You” Emmy nominee
body:
HBO‘s “Harry Potter” showrunner Francesca Gardiner is condemning the “abuse” being directed at Paapa Essiedu, the “I May Destroy You” Emmy nominee who is taking over the role of Professor Severus Snape in the first television series adaptation of J.K. Rowling‘s literary franchise. Essiedu has been outspoken since March about the racism he’s been facing online by toxic fans upset with the casting of a Black actor in the role. 

	“It’s appalling that anyone should be subjected to that kind of abuse in any circumstances,” Gardiner told Vanity Fair as part of a new profile on the actor. “He has handled it with incredible grace, and I have nothing but the greatest respect for him…. Paapa has absolutely nailed the role, and it is that performance that deserves our attention.”
	

	Essiedu told the publication that he is more than open to criticism when it is warranted, explaining: “There’s some people who are just like, ‘I’ve done my research, and I know what kind of actor you are, and you suck.’ And they’re totally entitled to their opinion. But then there are the people who are like, ‘You are bad because you are Black’—which, to me, is racist.. Well, actually not ‘You’re bad because you are Black.’ But there is a racially driven animosity.”

	Essiedu first spoke to The Sunday Times in March about the racially motivated death threats he was getting online over his casting as Snape.

	“I’ve been told, ‘Quit or I’ll murder you,’” Essiedu he said at the time. “The reality is that if I look at Instagram I will see somebody saying, ‘I’m going to come to your house and kill you.’ So while I’m pretty sure I’m not going to be murdered…That could age badly! But, yes, while I hope I’ll be OK, nobody should have to encounter this for doing their job. Many people put their lives on the line in their work. I’m playing a wizard in ‘Harry Potter.’ And I’d be lying if I said it doesn’t affect me emotionally.”
	

	Speaking to Variety last month at the TIME100 Next Gala, Essiedu said “the whole team” behind HBO’s “Harry Potter” has “has been so supportive of me” in the wake of racist abuse.

	“Obviously, my priority is the work. I wouldn’t take this job on [otherwise], but I walk into it with open eyes,” he added “I understand the broad spectrum of what the reaction to what we’re doing means, and I take that mantle on with an open and full heart. I’ve also been blown away by a lot of the support and well-wishes and excitement… I’m really proud of what I’ve seen so far. There are so many people who worked so hard on this project — and who it means so much to. It’s been a long time coming. It’s been a long time that people have been saying a lot of things, and now’s the time for people to engage with what we made.”

	Essiedu also spoke to Vanity Fair about his outspoken support for the trans community, which fans speculate put him at odds with “Harry Potter” author J.K. Rowling. Before his casting, Essiedu signed an open letter condemning the U.K. Supreme Court for ruling that transgender women are not legally considered women and transgender men are not legally considered men.

	“I don’t have the power to sack an actor from the series and I wouldn’t exercise it if I did,” Rowling wrote on X in May while sharing an article about Essiedu. “I don’t believe in taking away people’s jobs or livelihoods because they hold legally protected beliefs that differ from mine.”

	Rowling has courted controversy since 2020 for regularly sharing beliefs on social media that many believe are transphobic. When the topic of the author was brought up by Vanity Fair, Essiedu responded: “I don’t want to talk about Jo at all.”

	“I believe, in my bones, that trans people, queer people, people of all creeds and color have got the right to be treated with respect and dignity and safety at all times— whether they’re in the workplace, whether they’re at home or in the street, whatever,” Essiedu said. “That’s what I believe, and that’s the way that I choose to live my life. That’s the creed by which I live.”

	“Harry Potter” debuts Christmas Day on HBO and HBO Max.

schema.headline: ‘Harry Potter’ Star Paapa Essiedu Says ‘I Don’t Want to Talk About’ J.K. Rowling ‘At All’ but ‘Trans People Have the Right to Be Treated With Respect and Dignity’

title: ‘It’s Hotter Than Mordor’: On Set for ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3, Where Dwarf Beards Are Falling Off Under a U.K. Heatwave
description:
British heatwaves and massive, thick dwarven beards, perhaps unsurprisingly, don’t mix well together.

	We’re inside a soundstage at Shepperton Stu
body:
British heatwaves and massive, thick dwarven beards, perhaps unsurprisingly, don’t mix well together.

	We’re inside a soundstage at Shepperton Studios in late June for Season 3 of Prime Video’s “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power,” and with mercury levels topping 90 degrees and wildfire alerts across Greater London, the residents of the dwarf kingdom of Khazad-dûm are facing a dastardly new villain: sweat.


	But help is at hand, literally. Almost every cast and crew member, numbering in the hundreds, is holding a mini fan. If a fan isn’t spotted in the back of a shot (remember the “Game of Thrones” coffee cup?), it’ll be a miracle.
	

	Cameras are getting ready to roll, and before Owain Arthur — who plays newly crowned dwarf King Durin IV — steps onto a set that looks like it been carved out of the Misty Mountains themselves, one assistant holds a mini fan directly in front his face while another points one at the back of his neck.

	For all the valiant efforts, the battle against the intense heat isn’t always victorious.

	“Eddie Marsan’s beard suddenly peeled off in a close-up yesterday,” notes hair and make-up designer Flora Moody. “We’re really try to keep things on, but it’s a struggle — everyone’s just sweating so much.”

	While few may have foreseen an early summer heatwave such as this, Moody hasn’t exactly helped matters. To reflect Season 3 jumping ahead five years after Season 2, she upped the volume of on-screen hair considerably.

	“I think this is one of the hairiest shows,” she suggests. As a result, the dwarf beards — made of yak tail hair (quite itchy, apparently) — are bulkier, longer and often more elaborate plaited. Crucially, they’re heavier, so when the glue holding them in place mixes with sweat, they are more liable to slip off.
	



	

	



	It’s not any easier for the prosthetics team, which is desperately trying to stop the same fate as Marsan’s beard happening to their oversized dwarven noses and ears.

	“When you’re getting somebody into a thick layer of rubber and then covering them in really heavy leather costumes, they’re just walking saunas,” says Barrie Gower, who, alongside his wife Sarah Gower, has overseen the creation of the thousands of body parts being used across the show. “We’re probably one of the most irritating departments for the actors and supporting artists, because we spend the entire day walking around and prodding their faces to try to preventing things from peeling off them.”

	Inside Khazad-dûm, more elaborate dwarven cooling technologies have also been deployed. 

	“We had ice vests,” notes Marsan, speaking after the shoot. The veteran actor joins “Rings of Power” Season three as Thrain — a power-hungry dwarf looking to claim the throne from his younger brother Durin IV (who was only given it following the climactic finale of Season 2, when his dad sacrificed himself to keep a balrog at bay).

	Powered by battery, the thin ice vests “have water channels, a little bit like an electric blanket,” says costume designer Libby Dempster, upped to lead for Season 3 and also part of the fight to hold back sweat. “You plug them in between takes and they’re attached to an ice pack.”

	But, of course, ice packs didn’t prevent Marsan’s beard-slip moment.

	A short electric buggy ride away outside another soundstage, a group of orcs — fully kitted out in scraggly armor, prosthetic faces and terrifying fake eyes are fanning themselves under a tiny amount of shade. Asked how they’re coping, one — almost scripted — bellows: “It’s hotter than the fiery pits of Mordor!”

	The heatwave is, of course, being felt across the whole of Middle-earth. But the elves — less weighed down by volumous hair and with wardrobes not so focussed on bulk — aren’t facing quite the same issue. “We didn’t suffer as much as others,” notes Morfydd Clark, who plays Galadriel, after the shoot. However, she says the costume department did find it tricky to “keep the elves looking effortlessly cool while we’re all a bit a sweaty and red.”
	

	That said, Robert Aramayo, playing Elrond, got away with it almost entirely. “He’s the luckiest of the elves, because he doesn’t have a wig,” Clark notes with a comic twang of jealousy. “He just has such a gorgeous natural head of hair.”


	Heat — unplanned or not — is something of a theme for “The Rings of Power” Season 3, where over in the fiery volcano of Mount Doom arguably the most seismic event in Tolkien’s entire universe is taking place.

	Yes, it’s the forging of the One Ring to Rule Them All by the Dark Lord Sauron himself. As showrunner J.D. Payne says, it’s a hotly anticipated moment that allows Charlie Vickers, having spent the previous two seasons in disguise as Halbrand and Annatar, to finally make his grand long-in-the-works entrance as “full metal Sauron” (with a fancy new sword, too).

	Of course, such a momentous occasion — one that will shift the entire story of the series (and, you know, potentially play a part in future plotlines involving Hobbitses) wasn’t one where the filmmakers wanted to go minimal. Fellow “Rings of Power” co-showrunner Patrick McKay describes the ring-making scene they shot as “the most extraordinarily technically complicated sequence we’ve ever attempted on the show,” one that even VFX specialist Jason Smith (an Oscar nominee for the bear sequences on “The Revenant”) said was one of the most complex of his career.

	And yet, perhaps offsetting some of this lava-enhanced lurch towards evil, a very different sort of heat is steaming things up elsewhere.

	Payne admits that Galadriel has “been through the ringer” so far in “The Rings of Power,” so this time around they’re brightening things up for her with a splash of romance. “From the very beginning, we had a plan to bring back her long-lost husband, who she believes is dead, and this was the season to tell that love story,” he says.

	“It’s just lush,” says Clark, adding that it was nice to take a break from the battlefield to spend some time in the “magical fairy realm.”

	And in Jamie Campbell Bower, who plays her returning spouse Celeborn (found after a six-month casting process), she says the show has “managed to find an actual real-life elf.”

	Things may be looking for Galadriel in Season 3 (aside from the whole Sauron thing, of course) but it’s about to get worse for poor Elrond. The showrunners previously stated that they planned to “break” the youthful, ambitious diplomat seen so far to set him on the path towards the stoic, battle-hardened leader as depicted in the films, and it looks like that’s happening this time.

	“They’re constantly testing him — all the time he’s morally grappling with the challenges they’re giving him,” says Aramayo.
	


	The first season of “The Rings of Power” shot during lockdown in New Zealand, arguably the closest country to Middle-earth thanks to Peter Jackson’s efforts. But it shifted to the U.K. — home to a good number of the main cast and heads of department — for the second, mostly divided between Bovingdon Airfield and Bray Studios (which Amazon later acquired and — if rumors are correct — was recently used to hold the final James Bond auditions).

	For Season 3, they’ve shifted the entire operation into the newly-expanded Shepperton Studios (which wasn’t ready for Season 2), taking over nine of the 17 new soundstages and a backlot. Funnily enough, Netflix had already moved into the other eight, which it uses to house “Bridgerton” (a mere white fence divides too very different shows).



	

	



	It’s a hugely impressive setup here. And it’s one, given the worlds and characters being created, that offers some truly wonderful visual moments. Witnessing a group of orcs tuck into craft services (an impressive selection of dishes with each listed on a board alongside their carbon footprint) is a sight that should never get old.

	Barring some major upheaval, there won’t be any further relocating. “Season 3 and going forward, we are all in Shepperton,” says McKay. But the vast size and scope of the facility the series now calls home does mean that almost everything can be shot there.

	“I think the biggest thing for this season is that we’re not going to go abroad and shoot big foreign landscapes, we’re going to do a lot more here,” says production designer Kristian Milstead, who notes that, while while some of the set builds for Season 3 might not be the biggest on the show, one is certainly the most immersive, allowing for camera shots in all directions (and thus drastically reducing the need for any extension into VFX).


	For all the impressive creativity — and creative cooling methods — there is a small oliphaunt in the room.

	The “Rings of Power” is widely considered to be the most expensive TV show ever produced, with a reported price tag in the region of $1 billion, way above the likes of “House of the Dragon” or “Stranger Things.”

	And yet, despite the record-breaking investment, it hasn’t quite left the cultural mark on the world the team behind it — nor Jeff Bezos himself — might have hoped for. Alongside middling reviews and a backlash from some Tolkien fans, audience numbers have dwindled since its impressive launch (Season 2 had a 60% drop off from Season 1).

	“I think with anyone who is shepherding a title or piece of IP with a huge global audience, you have to be your own harshest critic,” says Payne when asked about dealing with exterior noise. “The pressure we put on ourselves as fans of this material — that has been be the God we pray to.”

	Given the cost and reaction, there has been questions over whether Prime Video will continue “The Rings of Power.” Amazon originally committed to a five-season, 50-episode run, but Season 4 is yet to be officially greenlit, despite rumors it’s shooting in early 2027.
	

	“We’re busily working away in Middle-earth every day,” says McKay diplomatically when asked if he’s confident the show will get the full five-season run. “We just keep going.” 

	Clark, meanwhile, simply appreciates that shows as bold, elaborate and as “The Rings of Power” are actually being made.

	“I just love to be on something creative where there’s a couple of thousand people employed to do it, it’s just wonderful,” she says. “That’s why I’m always so happy when we have another season because the amount of people that are a part of making it is just massive. So I just feel really lucky to be heading back into this world, but also heading back into it with this village that we’ve got.”

title: The Business of Being a Business Manager; ‘The Secret Reading Club of Kabul’ Directors on Finding Inspiration and Courage
description: On today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, host Cynthia Littleton breaks down the complicated business of being a business manage
body:
On today’s episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, host Cynthia Littleton breaks down the complicated business of being a business manager for clients who work in media and entertainment.

	Variety is set to publish its annual Business Managers Elite feature section, in print and online on Nov. 11, highlighting the industry’s top financial and accounting mavens who have their finger on the pulse of trends in entertainment and important macro-economy issues. 
	

	“Business managers are the Swiss army knives of personal representatives. Business managers do a lot more than pay the bills, especially for people who work in entertainment. Compensation can be lumpy. In some cases, the client gets paid with big upfront fees. In others, royalty and residual payments trickle down for years, if not decades,” Littleton observes. “Business managers have to connect with all the people in their clients lives, From investors and family offices to tax advisers, lawyers, agents, managers, doctors and coaches.”

	Business managers are also often pressed into service as consiglieris on major transactions. This year’s top honoree is Citrin Cooperman veteran Arnie Herrmann. In the profile set to publish Nov. 11, Herman tells me that he finds real estate is one of the most emotional decisions that people make. Sometimes he has to guide people through the fact that they’re overpaying for a property. Sometimes they’re OK with that, and it’s Herman’s job to make sure that they have all the facts.

	This episode also features highlights of Variety‘s “Doc Dreams” event held Nov. 9 in New York. The gathering features conversations with top documentarians, including Alex Gibney, the helmer and producer behind “Musk,” the controversial deep dive on Elon Musk. One of the most powerful discussions was held with Shakiba Adil and Elina Hirvonen, co-directors of “The Secret Reading Club of Kabul.” The two explain how the writings of Anne Frank more than 80 years before inspired them and the docu subjects to chronicle the horrors of living under the Taliban regime in Afghanistan.
	

	“I had moved to Finland some years back, and a Finnish friend gave me ‘The Diary of Anne Frank,’ ” Adil explains. 

	“In the ’90s, when I was in Afghanistan, when the Taliban took over, I was told that I cannot go to school. And I always wondered if the world know what happened to us. Does anybody know what is going on in Afghanistan? Has everybody forgotten us? I always missed my school friends and I wondered what happened,” she says. “And when I got the book, I felt like, oh my God, there has been someone else also experiencing the same thing like as me. Because I thought that nobody understood us, the young women in Afghanistan. But then I read Anne Frank’s diary, and I realized that in the other side of the world, a young girl has experienced exactly similar thing, which is like everything is taken away and how your world becomes smaller and smaller.”

schema.headline: The Business of Being a Business Manager; ‘The Secret Reading Club of Kabul’ Directors on Finding Inspiration and Courage

title: Adobe Premiere Mobile App Launches Hundreds of Thousands of Tracks Licensed From UMG, WMG
description:
Adobe has just made it easier for creators to add some of their favorite hot jams to short-form video clips.

	On Tuesday, the free Adobe Premiere
body:
Adobe has just made it easier for creators to add some of their favorite hot jams to short-form video clips.

	On Tuesday, the free Adobe Premiere mobile app, designed for creators to make videos for platforms like YouTube Shorts, TikTok and Instagram Reels, added hundreds of thousands of songs licensed from Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group. Initially, the music tracks are available to users in the U.S., Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
	

	Top-trending tracks avaliable in the app at launch include:  Olivia Dean’s “So Easy (To Fall In Love)”; Sombr’s “Homewrecker”; Chappell Roan’s “Good Luck, Babe!”; Justin Bieber’s “Daisies”; Lady Gaga’s “The Dead Dance”; Ava Max’s “Sweet but Psycho”; Vance Joy’s “Riptide”; OneRepublic’s “Counting Stars”; and Teddy Swims’ “Lose Control.” 

	There’s a bit of a catch: The music from UMG and WMG is licensed to Premiere mobile app users for personal, non-commercial use. But in most cases, according to Adobe, the music has been cleared for use on YouTube Shorts and other platforms. (If you’re using Premiere mobile for projects that require commercially licensed music, you can also continue to access Adobe Stock Audio.)

	Users of Premiere on mobile can browse, search and preview trending music by artist or track; filter by genre and duration; bookmark favorites; and explore popular music through label-featured collections. Once they select a track, they can then add up to 60 seconds directly to their video. In addition, Premiere mobile provides customizable templates paired with music.

	“Adobe hasn’t built the music muscle before this,” Jay LeBoeuf, Adobe head of AI audio for creators, told Variety in an interview at the Adobe MAX 2026 creativity conference in Miami Beach.
	

	The pain point Adobe is addressing: Creators using Premiere on mobile haven’t had an easy way to add music to their videos in the editing stage. “Creators want to work with the songs and artists they love,” LeBoeuf said. According to a survey in June funded by Adobe that was conducted by the Berklee College of Music, 83.7% of creators said they have built a video around a selected song. But many also say they have encountered copyright issues in trying to use music in their videos, and that they often resort to using a royalty-free track instead.

	With the UMG and WMG deals, said LeBoeuf, “creators get access to the content they need in an approved way. It was important for us to have a legitimate deal with the labels.”

	“Good music is scarce,” he continued. “There’s a reason a certain song is driving a TikTok or Instagram trend.” Adobe is seeking additional licensing deals for music with other rightsholders.

	Bryan Stone, Universal Music Group’s senior VP of business development, said Adobe’s Premiere on mobile is the only creative application the music company has a licensing deal for in this way without a social component. Bringing licensed music from UMG artists into Adobe Premiere mobile gives creators new ways to build videos around the songs they love while helping UMG’s artists and songwriters reach new audiences, he said.

	“We are excited about being at that level of deepening the relationship with creators. We know that music is where creators start,” Stone said.

	In a statement, Rachel Scarpati, WMG’s VP of digital strategy and business development, said, “The way people experience and engage with music extends far beyond traditional listening platforms. Our partnership with Adobe Premiere mobile integrates WMG’s catalog directly into the creative process, opening up new possibilities for creative expression and deeper fan engagement.”

	The Premiere mobile app provides video-editing tools, “studio-quality” audio tools like Enhance Audio to reduce distracting background noise and Adobe Firefly-powered AI features to generate creative assets. The app is free to download and use (with no watermarks inserted); users can purchase credits for gen-AI image, video and sound effects created with Firefly.

title: Florence Pugh Says ‘I’m Not Standing for Bulls— Behavior’ on Set Anymore: ‘Show Up on Time, Don’t Be Rude, Don’t Be a Misogynist’
description: Florence Pugh said in a new interview with Elle magazine that it’s taken time for her to learn how to lead a film set and she is no longer acceptin
body:
Florence Pugh said in a new interview with Elle magazine that it’s taken time for her to learn how to lead a film set and she is no longer accepting “bullshit” when it comes to her fellow casts and crews.

	“Every time I work on a movie, I get more confident in the way that I can protect myself and the way that I can lead a film set, and just not stand for bullshit anymore. I’m not doing it,” Pugh said. “I’m not standing for bullshit behavior. I’m not standing for bullshit attitude. I’m not allowing for people to be rude to the crew. You just get bolder and bigger and more confident with time, and you want to be around and work with the right people. And the moment someone is making that vibe feel off, everybody feels it.”
	

	“I don’t want to deal with messy,” the Oscar nominee continued. “It’s just about surrounding yourself with professionals who have the same way of working in mind: Show up on time, don’t be rude, don’t be a misogynist.”

	Pugh is having a standout end to the year thanks to her acclaimed performance on Netflix’s “East of Eden,” which will be followed by two expected blockbusters with the Dec. 18 releases of “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part Three.” And yet, the actor seemingly generated the most headlines this year  for publicly condemning the Cornell 7, the name given online to the seven male students accused of drugging and gang raping their female classmate at Cornell University in October 2024. Pugh called out Instagram for censoring her initial posts on the matter.

	“No one fucking censors me,” she now told Elle magazine. “Don’t even try. That’s just going to add fuel to the fire.”
	

	Pugh said she was compelled to be so outspoken about the Cornell allegations “because I’m a woman who cares about women. I care about women I know, and I care about women I don’t know. And if we allow for stories like that to become in any way normal, then we are allowing ourselves to continue toward that destiny of abuse and rape being accepted as a norm.” 

	Pugh continued, “Rape can never ever be a conversation that we move on from. It has to be something that we look at, face-on, and we demand justice, accountability, and for the rapist to see what they have done to someone’s life. Because if we don’t, we’re accepting it. And I don’t ever, ever, ever want to live in a world where we move on from it easily.”

	Head over to Elle Magazine’s website to read Pugh’s profile in its entirety.

schema.headline: Florence Pugh Says ‘I’m Not Standing for Bulls— Behavior’ on Set Anymore: ‘Show Up on Time, Don’t Be Rude, Don’t Be a Misogynist’

title: Pillsbury Doughboy Voice Actor JoBe Cerny Dead at 78
description:

body:
Pillsbury Doughboy Voice Actor
                          Dead at 78
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 10, 2026
                            10:34 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 10, 2026
                                12:12 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            JoBe Cerny, the man who brought the iconic Pillsbury Doughboy to life with his unmistakable voice, has died after a lengthy battle with Alzheimer's disease ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Cerny's son, Tim Cerny, tells TMZ ... his dad, best known for voicing the baking mascot and its signature giggle, died October 30 in Illinois.
      
    
            Tim says his father was diagnosed with Alzheimer's around 2020 and had to step away from voicing the Pillsbury Doughboy around that time as his health declined.
      

            Cerny spent decades entertaining audiences, but his most recognizable role was lending his voice to the Pillsbury Doughboy, also known as Poppin' Fresh ... the white mascot famous for giggling when poked in the belly.
      
    
            Cerny appeared in thousands of commercials and other productions over more than five decades ... including serving as the silent spokesperson for Cheer detergent.
      
    
            His family says outside of show business, Cerny loved racing go-karts and collecting model trains.
      
    
            He was 78.
      
    
            RIP.
